paper_did: Synthesized a bulk Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 high‐entropy alloy via mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS).

Characterized the microstructure using X‐ray diffraction (XRD), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and scanning TEM to reveal a primary fcc (γ) matrix embedded with hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates (primary γ′ and secondary γ* phases) along with a minor bcc phase.

Performed in situ mechanical tests – including SEM microtensile testing and in situ TEM compression – to measure ultrahigh tensile performance (yield strength ~1.86 GPa, ultimate strength ~2.52 GPa, failure strain ~5.2%) and to observe dislocation motions (specifically, dislocation shearing through coherent precipitates).
Applied nonequilibrium thermodynamic (Scheil-Gulliver) modeling and discussed the role of precipitation strengthening via dislocation shearing as the dominant strengthening mechanism.
paper_reported: The formation of a hierarchical nanoprecipitate architecture in the fcc matrix, with γ′ precipitates having an average size of ~57 nm and an inter-precipitate spacing averaging ~11 nm, and an overall precipitate volume fraction of ~51%.

Ultrahigh tensile strength with a significant work-hardening behavior and an appreciable failure strain (~5.2%) attributed to coherent precipitation strengthening, where dislocations shear both the primary (γ′) and secondary (γ*) nanoprecipitates.
Evidence from in situ TEM tests confirming that the dislocation propagation through the fcc matrix involves shearing of nanoprecipitates, thus reinforcing the precipitation strengthening mechanism.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests that the design strategy employing a high density of hierarchical nanoprecipitates can be applied to develop HEAs (or other multicomponent alloys) with ultrahigh strength.
It encourages further investigations into processing parameters and microstructural architectures to optimize the trade-off between strength and ductility in advanced alloy systems.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A rapid prediction method for HfNbTiVAl10’s mechanical properties can be developed by integrating high‐resolution digital image correlation (DIC) measurements during tensile testing to extract local microstrain gradients that correlate with the underlying hierarchical nanoprecipitate architecture.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure (coherent nanoprecipitates embedded in a matrix) similar in spirit to the microstructural architecture reported in Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15.
hypotheses.intervention: Implement in situ tensile experiments combined with high-resolution DIC to capture local strain fields and gradients; then develop a reduced-order analytical model that uses these measured strain heterogeneities to predict macroscopic Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture initiation parameters.
hypotheses.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature under displacement-controlled conditions on specimens with well-prepared surfaces; the DIC system must have sufficient spatial resolution to resolve strain localization at the nanoprecipitate level.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The local strain fields are modulated by the dense distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates, which hinder dislocation motion via the shearing mechanism.
hypotheses.mechanism: Hierarchical nanoprecipitates act as obstacles that create detectable local strain gradients. By measuring these gradients, one can infer the degree of dislocation obstruction and, in turn, predict yield and fracture behavior more directly than by simulating complex microstructural mechanics.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to improve predictive efficiency by reducing computation time by 5–10× and enhance accuracy by 10–20% relative to standard finite element simulations, provided that the local microstrain features are strong indicators of the precipitate shearing resistance.
hypotheses.baseline: Conventional full-scale simulations (e.g., detailed finite element modeling) of tensile and fracture tests.
hypotheses.boundary: The approach may fail if the DIC resolution is insufficient to capture the fine-scale strain heterogeneity, or if extrinsic factors (such as surface imperfections or environmental conditions) mask the strain gradients.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative gains in accuracy and efficiency remain to be confirmed experimentally; while the relationship between local strain gradients and macroscopic properties is supported by literature, statistical correlation strength in HfNbTiVAl10 is uncertain.

hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes using local microstrain gradients captured by DIC as rapid, direct inputs for property prediction, bypassing extensive computational simulations while leveraging the physical microstructure–mechanics relationship.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Acoustic resonance measurements can serve as a rapid proxy to predict the Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture parameters in HfNbTiVAl10 by capturing the modifications in elastic wave propagation induced by its hierarchical heterostructure.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy with a hierarchical heterostructure featuring coherent nanoprecipitates that interact with elastic waves.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject samples to ultrasonic acoustic testing (e.g., pulse-echo measurements) to determine resonance frequencies and internal friction. Develop a model that correlates these acoustic signatures with the material’s mechanical properties.
hypotheses.conditions: Acoustic tests must be performed at controlled frequencies (in the MHz range) and temperatures with clean contact conditions. The sample must be free of macroscopic flaws that could dominate scattering.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The hierarchical arrangement of nanoprecipitates alters local stiffness and damping properties, modulating acoustic wave scattering and resonance behavior.
hypotheses.mechanism: Coherent nanoprecipitates change the effective elastic stiffness (and hence acoustic velocity) via dislocation-precipitate interactions that also control yield and fracture behavior. Shifts in resonance frequencies and attenuation coefficients provide a ‘signature’ of these microstructural features, enabling a rapid inverse determination of bulk mechanical properties.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The ultrasonic-acoustic method is expected to reduce testing time significantly (potentially by an order of magnitude relative to full mechanical tests) and provide mechanical property predictions with a modest improvement (around 10–20% better accuracy) compared to established numerical simulations, given clear acoustic signatures.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard tensile and fracture tests or detailed simulation models of wave propagation in heterogeneous media.
hypotheses.boundary: The method may yield inaccurate predictions if the acoustic signals are confounded by extrinsic factors (e.g., sample porosity, surface roughness) or if the nanoprecipitate distribution does not produce a distinct acoustic signature.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative link between elastic heterogeneity and acoustic properties is well known, the quantitative mapping to yield and fracture parameters in HfNbTiVAl10 remains to be precisely established.

fields.intervention: Design a tensile testing protocol that dynamically modulates the strain rate during a single test cycle (alternating between low and high strain rate segments) while continuously recording dynamic responses.

fields.mechanism: Different strain rates can activate or suppress specific deformation mechanisms in the hierarchical microstructure. High strain rate segments may accentuate dislocation inertia and transient local stress buildup while low strain rate segments allow for stress relaxation and redistribution. These differences manifest as measurable changes in resonance characteristics and acoustic emission patterns, which, when integrated into a physics-informed ML algorithm, serve as rapid surrogates for directly predicting bulk properties such as Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
fields.predicted_outcome: The ML framework is expected to yield property predictions within an error margin of ±15% as compared to conventional tensile and fracture tests, and will reduce prediction time by approximately 40–50% relative to established simulation methods.
fields.baseline: Standard tensile tests at a constant strain rate, followed by computationally intensive simulations to predict mechanical properties.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis may fail if the dynamic signals generated by strain rate modulation are too subtle, become masked by noise, or if the intrinsic homogeneous microstructure does not respond differently enough to varied strain rates to produce unique, predictive signatures.

fields.boundary: The approach may fail if the ultrasonic frequency is not adequately tuned to the heterogeneity scale or if calibration does not capture nonlinearity at very high dislocation densities; also, extreme oxidation effects (during high-temperature tests) are not addressed.
fields.uncertainty: Absolute quantitative gains in prediction accuracy depend on the quality of calibration and test resolution; while the general trend is supported, precise percentages require experimental determination.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: fracture mechanics principles that relate local stress concentrations (due to micro-notches) to fracture toughness (TXT::wikipedia::Fracture_mechanics::022) and on the paper’s observations of uniform dislocation slip indicating fracture behavior is not obscured by inhomogeneous yielding.
pool.what_is_new: It isolates and exploits local strain localization near controlled micro-notches, using high-resolution DIC to rapidly assess fracture-related properties without the resource-intensiveness of full-field crack propagation simulations.

fields.hypothesis: Controlled micro-notch introduction coupled with high-resolution digital image correlation (DIC) can rapidly determine the local fracture toughness of HfNbTiVAl10, which correlates with overall fracture behavior under tensile loading without the full computational cost of simulating crack propagation.
fields.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure and homogeneous dislocation slip behavior as observed in uniform tensile testing.
fields.intervention: Create micro-notches (or pre-cracks) on tensile specimens using focused ion beam (FIB) milling. Subject these specimens to uniaxial tensile loading while capturing high-speed DIC data to resolve strain fields and crack-tip plastic zone evolution.
fields.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature and at strain rates typical for tensile testing; notch dimensions will be on the order of a few micrometers to mimic relevant flaw sizes.
fields.structural_mediator: The micro-notch acts as an artificial crack initiator whose local strain concentration interacts with the alloy’s microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., dislocation density variations, dendritic boundaries) to govern early crack initiation and propagation.
fields.mechanism: Focusing the analysis on the near-tip region, DIC captures rapid strain localization and the development of the fracture process zone. These local measurements are then statistically correlated with bulk fracture toughness (e.g., crack initiation stress, crack tip opening displacement). By doing so, the test bypasses the need for full-scale simulation of global crack propagation. This method leverages fracture mechanics principles (TXT::wikipedia::Fracture_mechanics::022) and does not assume that yield behavior is driven by the notch but focuses instead on fracture-related behavior.
fields.predicted_outcome: The DIC analysis is expected to yield a rapid estimation of fracture toughness parameters that correlate within ±10% of those measured by full-scale tensile and fracture tests, significantly reducing the time and computational resources required.
fields.baseline: Conventional fracture testing and finite element simulations of crack initiation and propagation in bulk specimens.
fields.boundary: This method may fail if the artificially introduced notch does not adequately represent natural flaws in the material or if the DIC spatial resolution is insufficient to capture the fine details of the strain gradients near the notch tip.
fields.uncertainty: While fracture toughness estimation via DIC is supported by fracture mechanics theory, the exact statistical correlation between local notch behavior and bulk fracture properties requires calibration and may vary with notch geometry.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fracture toughness predicted from notched specimen DIC analysis deviates by more than 10% from the bulk measurements over multiple tests, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The paper’s discussion on the influence of cooling rate and annealing conditions on B2 LRO and mechanical properties.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis suggests deliberately engineering a spatial gradient in microstructure to rapidly generate a calibrated dataset for predicting tensile and fracture behavior, rather than relying exclusively on time-consuming simulations.

fields.hypothesis: Spatially modulating the hierarchical heterostructure via a controlled gradient in cooling rate will induce predictable local variations in B2 ordering that, when mapped using rapid scanning mechanical tests, enable faster and more accurate prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
fields.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 with a naturally occurring hierarchical heterostructure featuring regions of varying B2 order.
fields.intervention: Implement a spatial cooling-rate gradient during casting (or subsequent heat treatment) to deliberately produce a continuous gradient in local B2 LRO across the sample.
fields.conditions: Prepare samples with a known cooling rate gradient; perform localized (e.g., micro-tensile or indentation-based tensile) tests across regions of different LRO; quantify local microstructure using electron microscopy and correlatively map mechanical property variations.
fields.structural_mediator: Spatial variation in the degree of B2 LRO controlled by the cooling rate.
fields.mechanism: A higher cooling rate is expected to suppress B2 LRO formation, yielding regions with lower yield strength and possibly a lower modulus, while slower cooled regions develop stronger B2 LRO, increasing strength but reducing ductility. Rapid mapping of these variations provides a database linking localized microstructural states to mechanical responses, thereby refining predictive ML models faster than running full simulations.
fields.predicted_outcome: A measurable spatial correlation (e.g., differences on the order of 10–20% in yield strength and modulus between high and low LRO regions) between cooling-induced microstructural variations and local mechanical properties that can be rapidly captured. ML models using these spatially correlated datasets should predict the overall tensile and fracture behavior with improved speed and accuracy.
fields.baseline: Conventional simulations assume a uniform microstructure and require extensive computation to account for heterogeneities.
fields.boundary: Should the cooling gradient fail to produce a significant variation in B2 LRO due to dominant nucleation kinetics or homogenization during solidification, the predictive gain may not materialize.
fields.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of property variation induced by the gradient is uncertain and may depend on processing nuances; further calibration across multiple samples is necessary.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant spatial differences in LRO are not observed or if the corresponding local mechanical properties do not correlate (e.g., R^2 < 0.5 between LRO level and yield/modulus) with the cooling-rate gradient, the hypothesis would be falsified.

pool.what_is_new: It proposes a hybrid approach that combines direct microstructural imaging and early-stage mechanical signals with machine learning to rapidly predict bulk mechanical properties, a method not covered by the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: An integrated machine learning framework that ingests quantitative microstructural descriptors from high-resolution microscopy (SEM/TEM) and correlates them with early-stage stress–strain signals can rapidly and accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture properties of HfNbTiVAl10.
fields.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy characterized by a hierarchical heterostructure with coherent nanoprecipitates and corresponding multiscale microstructural features.
fields.intervention: Acquire high-resolution images to extract descriptors (e.g., grain size, nanoprecipitate size/distribution, inter-precipitate spacing) and couple these with initial parts of stress–strain curves obtained from micro-tensile tests. Train a supervised machine learning model to map these features to full mechanical properties.
fields.conditions: Data collection must cover a sufficiently diverse set of samples, with controlled processing to ensure comparable hierarchical microstructures. The imaging and mechanical tests must be performed under standardized conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The hierarchical microstructure, particularly the size and spatial distribution of nanoprecipitates and grains, directly influences the dominant dislocation interactions (i.e., shearing versus bypass) that govern global stiffness and strength.
fields.mechanism: Variations in nanoprecipitate metrics (size, coherence, spacing) and initial stress–strain response capture intrinsic signatures of the dislocation-obstacle interactions noted in PMC6184785. By training a model on these features, one can bypass time-consuming full-scale simulations, achieving rapid predictions of mechanical properties.
fields.predicted_outcome: The ML framework should enable prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture parameters with a computational speed increase (reducing prediction time potentially by 90% relative to detailed simulations) and prediction error within an acceptable range (tentatively within ±20% of experimental values).
fields.baseline: Full finite element simulations and conventional experimental testing schemes.
fields.boundary: The approach may fail if the microstructural descriptors do not capture all essential features (e.g., effect of subtle chemical gradients) or if the training dataset is too limited or non-representative, undermining model generalizability.
fields.uncertainty: Exact predictive gains and error margins depend heavily on the quality and volume of input data; while the physical basis is clear, the statistical robustness across varied processing conditions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Collect a dataset of HfNbTiVAl10 samples with varied hierarchical microstructures using high-resolution SEM/TEM and perform early-stage tensile tests to capture initial stress–strain behavior. Train the ML model on a subset of the data and validate predictions against full mechanical test results on the remaining samples.

Initial and full stress–strain curves

top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the paper's success in using enhanced data features to predict fracture properties, extending the concept by incorporating transient, real-time AE signals to capture microstructural failure processes.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces the novel integration of high-frequency acoustic emission data into tensile testing of a high-entropy alloy, providing a dynamic and additional set of features for predicting mechanical properties more rapidly and accurately than traditional simulation methods.

fields.hypothesis: Integrating high-frequency acoustic emission (AE) monitoring into standard tensile tests of HfNbTiVAl10 will capture real-time microstructural failure events that provide additional, more sensitive predictors of yield strength and impending fracture. The fusion of these dynamic AE signatures with conventional tensile data in a machine learning model will enable faster and more accurate predictions of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior than established simulations.
fields.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 as produced, exhibiting a complex hierarchical heterostructure whose micro-crack initiation and propagation events are not fully captured by conventional slow mechanical testing.
fields.intervention: Attach high-sensitivity acoustic emission sensors to tensile test specimens to record transient signals during loading, in parallel with standard load-displacement measurements.
fields.conditions: Conduct standard uniaxial tensile tests at controlled loading rates while continuously recording AE signals; ensure proper sensor coupling and noise filtering in a laboratory setting.
fields.structural_mediator: The AE signals provide real-time insight into micro-crack nucleation, propagation events, and local energy releases that correlate with microstructural heterogeneities.
fields.mechanism: Acoustic emission monitoring detects the early microstructural events leading up to yield and fracture, thereby offering additional features (such as event frequency, amplitude, and energy) that can be correlated with macroscopic mechanical properties. When these AE parameters are integrated with conventional tensile data in a machine learning framework, the resulting predictive model can more rapidly and accurately forecast global mechanical behavior, effectively bridging the gap between measurable macro responses and complex internal damage evolution.
fields.predicted_outcome: The combination of AE data with tensile test measurements is expected to reduce the time required for comprehensive mechanical characterization and improve prediction accuracy (with error margins approaching or below 10%), surpassing established simulation approaches, especially under quasi-static conditions.
fields.baseline: Established simulation-based predictions and standard tensile tests that do not incorporate dynamic AE information.
fields.boundary: This approach might fail if the AE signals are dominated by noise or if the events recorded are not strongly correlated with the damaging microstructural processes—in particular, under conditions where loading rates are too low to trigger significant AE activity.
fields.uncertainty: The degree of quantitative improvement in predictive accuracy is uncertain due to the challenges in AE signal interpretation; however, directional improvement (faster, more accurate predictions) is expected if successful signal extraction is achieved.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of tensile tests on HfNbTiVAl10 specimens with integrated AE sensors. Process the AE data to extract features such as event count, amplitude, and energy, and combine these with standard tensile measurements in a machine learning model. Compare the predictive accuracy and speed of the AE-enhanced model to that of models based solely on conventional measurements.
measurements: AE event frequency, amplitude, and energy during loading
Standard load-displacement data, yielding Young's modulus and yield strength
Fracture toughness from post-failure analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive model that incorporates AE data does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in prediction error (i.e., error reduction of at least ~10%) or speed compared to the model based solely on conventional tensile testing, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C8
top3.builds_on: The established framework of combining CPA and MLIPs for bcc refractory MPEAs (PMC11275555::web::005–007) with the concept of universal bonding captured by virtual bond functions (PMC11275555::web::020–021), extended here via transfer learning.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a physics-informed transfer learning strategy that reuses simulation data from related alloys to rapidly predict the mechanical properties of HfNbTiVAl10, thereby reducing computational overhead and accelerating prediction—an approach not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A physics‐informed transfer learning approach that adapts pre‐trained models from similar bcc multi‐principal element alloys to the HfNbTiVAl10 system can accelerate and enhance predictions of its tensile and fracture properties.
fields.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, which shares key bonding and crystal symmetry characteristics with other bcc MPEAs (e.g., MoNbTiTa) previously studied.
fields.intervention: Utilize an existing dataset and machine‐learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) developed for bcc MPEAs to pre‐train a neural network model that predicts elastic constants and defect energies. Then, fine‐tune this model using a modest set of HfNbTiVAl10–specific simulation data (obtained via CPA and MTP calculations), while enforcing physics-based constraints (e.g., universal virtual bond functions, conservation of elastic energy) so that the model captures both common bonding physics and the unique influence of the hierarchical heterostructure in HfNbTiVAl10.
fields.conditions: The approach is applied under ambient testing conditions; the training dataset should contain a representative range of compositions and microstructural descriptors from both the pre‐training alloy systems and from HfNbTiVAl10, as confirmed by complementary experimental or high-fidelity simulation data.
fields.structural_mediator: Shared atomic bonding and crystal chemistry inherent to bcc alloys mediate the transfer of learned representations, while additional fine-tuning captures the mesoscale effects of the hierarchical heterostructure.
fields.mechanism: Transfer learning leverages common physical principles (e.g., bonding characteristics captured by virtual bond functions and elastic constants obtained via CPA) across similar alloys. By pre-training on data from analogous MPEAs and then fine-tuning with HfNbTiVAl10-specific corrections, the method circumvents the need for extensive new simulations. The physics-informed constraints ensure that the transfer respects known bonding behavior and interface effects, thereby accelerating prediction while maintaining accuracy.
fields.predicted_outcome: The transfer learning model is expected to reduce computational cost by up to 60% relative to full ab initio simulation workflows and achieve predictions for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness within ±10–15% of experimental benchmarks.
fields.baseline: Existing predictive models built from scratch solely on HfNbTiVAl10 data using full-scale simulations without leveraging prior data from similar alloys.
fields.boundary: The approach may fail if the fundamental bonding physics or microstructural influences in HfNbTiVAl10 diverge significantly from those in the pre-training dataset, or if the fine-tuning set is not sufficiently representative.
fields.uncertainty: The exact computational savings and prediction accuracy improvements depend on the quality and relevance of the pre-training data; estimated improvements (60% time reduction, ±10–15% accuracy) have inherent uncertainty and will require empirical validation.

Use the final model to predict tensile and fracture properties of HfNbTiVAl10. Compare these predictions with independent experimental measurements on HfNbTiVAl10 samples and evaluate computational cost savings against full-scale simulations.

top3.label: C3
top3.builds_on: the machine learning approach demonstrated in the paper, while using its transformer framework to include additional physics-based descriptors.
top3.what_is_new: Rather than just extending data volume for pre-training, this hypothesis focuses on enriching the input feature space with physics-informed tokens that capture local heterostructural effects, which are not explicitly modeled in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporating physics-informed feature tokens that encode local phase fractions and thermodynamic gradients within the hierarchical heterostructure of HfNbTiVAl10 into a transformer-based model will yield more rapid and accurate predictions of elastic, plastic, and fracture behavior.
fields.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy with a documented hierarchical heterostructure in its as-cast condition.
fields.intervention: Augment standard compositional descriptors with additional physics-informed parameters—such as locally estimated phase fractions, mixing enthalpy gradients, and modulus mismatches at heterostructural interfaces—and encode them as tokens for the transformer model.
fields.conditions: Data collected from samples under standardized tensile and fracture test conditions at room temperature; the physics-informed tokens are derived from complementary analysis (e.g., X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry) that quantify local thermodynamic states.
fields.structural_mediator: Local heterogeneity in phase composition and thermodynamic properties that govern the spatial stress distribution, influencing yield and fracture initiation sites.
fields.mechanism: By embedding physics-based descriptors that capture the heterogeneity of the microstructure (such as interfacial mixing enthalpy and modulus mismatches) into the transformer’s input, the model can more directly learn the causal relationships between local material states and global mechanical performance. This integration essentially bridges the gap between full-scale atomistic simulation and rapid prediction.
fields.predicted_outcome: A faster and more accurate prediction of mechanical properties (anticipated improvements in prediction time by a substantial factor, with accuracy gains in yield strength and fracture toughness predictions that meet or exceed ±10–15% error bounds compared to experiments).
fields.baseline: Conventional transformer-based or simulation methods that only consider global composition and average thermodynamic data without resolving local heterogeneity.
fields.boundary: The benefit is contingent on the accurate determination of local physics-informed tokens; if experimental quantification of local phase information is error-prone or inconsistent, the predictive advantage may be lost.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative gains and efficiency improvements remain somewhat uncertain without preliminary calibration studies of the additional tokens.

falsification_experiment.design: Create a transformer model with and without the added physics-informed tokens. Train both models on available HfNbTiVAl10 datasets and compare their predictions for tensile and fracture tests. Validate predictions with independent experimental measurements.
measurements: Prediction accuracy (R², MAE) for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness
Computation time for model inference
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the physics-informed model does not demonstrate a statistically superior performance and faster prediction times (beyond experimental uncertainty and typical simulation margins) relative to the baseline model, then the hypothesis is falsified.
